purpose: Record a proposed architectural decision for a synthetic event relay, its alternatives, consequences, and adoption gate.

facts.text: The synthetic event relay currently writes accepted events to a local append-only log before acknowledging the caller.
The relay has one active writer process and two read-only reporting processes in the exercise topology.
Definition: The exercise target is recovery after a single writer restart without losing acknowledged events.
A test with 10,000 synthetic events recovered the acknowledged sequence from the log after a writer restart.
The observed restart replay time in that test was 14 seconds on the exercise host.
Proposed: A proposed decision is to retain the append-only log as the recovery source for the next bounded pilot.
Proposed: The proposed pilot would add a checkpoint every 1,000 accepted events to bound replay work.
Proposed: An alternative under consideration is a shared database used as both intake and recovery store.
Assumed: The shared-database alternative would introduce a network dependency in the current single-host exercise topology.
Proposed: Another alternative is to rely on process memory and caller retries after a restart.
Caller retry IDs are present in 92 percent of the 10,000 synthetic requests, so memory-only recovery would leave unkeyed requests ambiguous.
Definition: The pilot acceptance criterion is exact recovery of acknowledged event IDs across three induced restarts.
Definition: The pilot acceptance criterion also requires duplicate suppression for requests with retry IDs.
The relay does not yet have a measured p99 recovery time across hosts.
Proposed: Checkpoint files are proposed to include a log position and checksum; the reader would reject a mismatched checksum.
The checkpoint format is not yet approved as a durable public compatibility contract.
Proposed: A proposed rollback is to disable checkpoint reads and replay the existing log from the beginning.
The decision is pending the three-restart pilot and a review of checkpoint corruption behavior.
